coverage.main: Read all sixteen pages of arXiv 2004.15015 (downloaded 25 September 2026): Sections 1-7, Tables 1-5, Figures 1-3, references and Appendices A-G (implementation, qualitative Table 6, cost calculation, suffix-dropper sentences, related work, angular-deviation Figure 4, API screenshots Figures 5-11). The EMNLP 2020 anthology version was not retrieved.
coverage.supplement: Appendices A-G are embedded in the arXiv PDF and read; they contain no additional transfer rates.
coverage.excluded_results: Tables 1-2 and Figure 3 (imitation fidelity BLEU and defended BLEU) and Table 5 (defense candidates) are model-stealing or defense outcomes. Table 3 and Appendix G screenshots are qualitative examples. The imitation-model columns of Table 4 are white-box.

result_groups.population: 200 WMT newstest2013 examples containing a token with a German antonym; targeted-flip and malicious-nonsense attacks on imitation models of Google, Bing and Systran (and a WMT14-trained Transformer Big for the Google baseline)
result_groups.outcome: transfer rate: 'the percent of successful attacks which are also successful on the production MT systems'
result_groups.evidence: The transfer rate is explicitly conditioned on attacks successful on the imitation model. A clean-correct event is not defined for translation outputs.

result_groups.population: The same 200 examples (Systran untargeted trigger) and 100 constructed prefix/suffix sentences (Bing suffix dropper, Appendix D)
result_groups.outcome: BLEU of the triggered output against the original output (5.46 versus 62.2/58.8 for random tokens); 76/100 dropped suffixes
result_groups.evidence: Universal phrases are applied to all inputs; source success per input is not defined for these outcomes.

result_groups.population: 400 IWSLT validation examples; malicious-nonsense attacks on imitation models trained against defended or undefended victims, plus a two-transformer baseline
result_groups.evidence: The same transfer-rate definition (percent of successful attacks that also succeed on the victim) is used.

f1.evidence: Clean BLEU of victim and imitation models is reported, which is positive baseline evidence, but a clean classification accuracy is not defined for token-flip or nonsense outcomes.

f2.evidence: No clean-correct analogue exists for these outcomes.

f3.evidence: Two scopes are explicitly source-success conditioned (yes); the universal-trigger scope is unresolved.

f4.evidence: The dropper result is an explicit count (76/100). Table 4 transfer rates are over unstated numbers of successful attacks (derivable only approximately from % Inputs x 200).

f5.evidence: Token replacement or appended phrases, reported as the percentage of changed tokens or phrase length; no L-infinity/L2 radius applies to discrete text. Reported in the non-image stratum.

f6.evidence: The linked fairseq-based attack code is released, but the targets are production APIs as of April 2020 and cannot be recomputed. Not executed.

artifact_checks.result: Linked in the paper. Listed via the GitHub API (386 files, head 1 May 2020): a fairseq fork with all_attack_utils.py. Imitation-model checkpoints and API outputs were not located. Not executed.

bounds_checks.reason: Translation flips, nonsense preservation and BLEU are not misclassification probabilities.

limitations: Non-blind evidence audit. Positive source-success conditioning is recorded for the flip/nonsense scopes.
